Q: FastAPI event loop blocked by Scikit-Learn Joblib thread-pool exhaustion during concurrent async inference A:

Two things.

1. Train outside the server. Move training to a separate script/notebook, persist with joblib.dump, and load the artifact via a lifespan event:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
import joblib

ml_models = {}

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    ml_models["clf"] = joblib.load("model.pkl")
    yield
    ml_models.clear()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

2. Your point 2 isn't accurate, and it's the whole problem.

I lose the parallelization benefits of the Random Forest, increasing single-request latency

n_jobs parallelizes across trees, not rows. One row through 100 shallow trees is tens of microseconds of work — dispatch costs more than the traversal. n_jobs=1 is likely faster here; benchmark it in isolation and your latency increase probably disappears.

So don't isolate the OpenMP pool — don't create it:

import os
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
os.environ["MKL_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
os.environ["OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
# must precede numpy/sklearn imports

model.set_params(n_jobs=1)

The env vars matter because n_jobs=1 won't stop BLAS from spawning its own pool (oversubscription docs; threadpoolctl if you'd rather set it at runtime).

Pattern: one thread per request, N concurrent requests, N cores busy. Also bump max_workers toward your core count — at 4 workers, 46 of your 50 requests are just queued.

For real throughput, batch: accumulate ~5ms of requests and predict on a (50, 10) array in one call. Same traversals, one dispatch — that's where n_jobs > 1 earns its keep.

Q: For a Jetpack Compose Textfield how can I show number keyboard but still allow user to switch to letters? A:

I just tried with the different options of keyboardType and found that by setting

KeyboardOptions(
    keyboardType = KeyboardType.Password,
)

The number buttons are added at the top of the text keyboard and not switching is required. Previously I was using KeyboardType.Text and the switching was necessary as you described. I'm not sure if this solution applies to all the devices.

Q: How do I automatically change from dark to light themes and back again in VS CODE? A:

Make it follow your OS theme. First option under "window" in VSCode settings -

https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/themes#_automatically-switch-based-on-os-color-scheme

Search for window.autoDetectColorScheme Or, paste this URL in your browser - vscode://settings/window.autoDetectColorScheme.

Then, just let your OS do the day/night switching. On mac os this can be done by setting the theme to "Auto".

Similar option probably exists on windows too.

Q: Content Security Policy causing 502 for WordPress admin login page A:

This is 2 years late so for the ones who are lost. Create a separate CSP polcy for /wp-admin/ URLS since it uses inline scripts extensively, even in 2026. Use a relaxed policy for /wp-admin/ and keep a strict csp for front end.

Other ways to make up for the relaxed policy in your admin dashboard:

  1. wp-config.php
// prevents theme/plugin editing from the dashboard
define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true ); 
// prevents administrators from injecting arbitrary HTML
define( 'DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML', true );
define( 'WP_AUTO_UPDATE_CORE', 'minor' );
define( 'FORCE_SSL_ADMIN', true );

2. Restrict /wp-admin/ access to specific IP addresses if you have a static IP via server level config

**
3. Monitor the /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php endpoint, which is often targeted by bots through WP Activity Log plugin

4. Really look over your file permission and enact ownership hardening**

4. Disable any access to wp-admin on server level configuration (i.e., .htaccess, nginx, etc).

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^wp-admin/includes/ - [F,L]
RewriteRule !^wp-includes/ - [S=3]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/[^/]+\.php$ - [F,L]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/js/tinymce/langs/.+\.php - [F,L]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/theme-compat/ - [F,L]
</IfModule>

Q: How to calculate relative volume (RVOL) efficiently in Postgres A:

Your sample SQL calculates the entire days' volumes repeating it for every core_price record then proceeds to average it over and over. It does not compare particular time slices across multiple days as you state you desire in your problem statement.

If you were truly following the calculation method outlined in your link you would limit the number of trading days to just the last two weeks and then create summarization buckets at the time interval you were interested in reporting at. For this example let's choose 5 minute intervals, as in the link you provided.

First in the inner SQL you should filter out anything older than 14 days and then create 5 minute buckets by day to directly sum your volumes into. Then in your outer SQL calculate your averages within each 5 minute interval. Since your timestamps are already expressed as EPOCHs in the data base, they are easy to calculate with that way:

Inner SQL:

Select symbol_id
    ,trunc((timestamp - Extract(EPOCH FROM CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) + 86400)/86400) as day
    , to_timestamp(trunc(timestamp%86400/(5*60))*5*60) as timeinterval
    , sum(volume) as dailyintervalvoume
From core_price
Where timestamp between Extract(EPOCH FROM CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '14 days') AND Extract(EPOCH FROM CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
Group By 1,3,2

Outer SQL:

Select symbol_id, timeinterval::time
    , Max(Case When day>=0 Then dailyintervalvoume End) as todayvolume
    , avg(dailyintervalvoume) as avgvolume
From (innersql)
Group By symbol_id, timeinterval

The inner SQL is where most of the interesting things happen. EPOCH is a convention in POSTGRESQL that is a timestampish format expressed as 'number of seconds since 1/1/1970'. Epoch divided by 86,400 is number of days since that event and Epoch % 86,400 {remainder) is number of seconds since midnight, no matter which day. The two '5*60' terms creates a timestamp rounded to 5 minute intervals that helps you put volume numbers into buckets. The Where clause limits the number of days you include in your average; here 14 days matches what is laid out in your link. The day field separates the different days' volumes but it also was normalized so that every past day would be negative and today (how I interpret your desire for 'current trading activity) would be zero. This allows the Case statement in the outer SQL to filter out all the past days and keep only the current day.

This SQL is more straightforward and should execute faster than your example. Note that the Where clause was specifically formulated to take advantage of any possible index that might exist on the timestamp field.

Q: How do browser-based website builders like Framer or Webflow communicate with a cross-origin iframe in real time? A:

No, professional editors do not send every drag event to the server. That would introduce unacceptable latency.

The common architecture is:

Editor (React)
        │
        │ Initial handshake
        ▼
Cross-origin iframe

During initialization, the editor typically establishes a dedicated communication channel.

A common pattern is:

  1. Create a MessageChannel.

  2. Transfer one MessagePort to the iframe using a single window.postMessage(...).

  3. After the handshake, communicate exclusively through the two MessagePorts.

For example:

const channel = new MessageChannel();

iframe.contentWindow.postMessage(
  { type: "connect" },
  iframeOrigin,
  [channel.port2]
);

// Continue communicating with:
channel.port1.postMessage(...);

The iframe receives the transferred port:

window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  const port = event.ports[0];

  port.onmessage = (e) => {
    // Receive updates
  };
});

This is generally preferable to continuously using window.postMessage() because:

  • it creates a dedicated communication channel,

  • avoids broadcasting messages to the entire window,

  • scales better,

  • and is commonly wrapped behind an internal RPC/transport abstraction.

For collaboration (multiplayer), many editors use a separate WebSocket connection—often backed by a CRDT such as Yjs or a custom implementation. The WebSocket synchronizes the shared document between clients, while the editor-to-iframe communication remains entirely local.

In other words:

  • Editor ↔ iframe: local messaging (MessageChannel / MessagePort)

  • Editor ↔ server: WebSocket + CRDT (for collaboration, autosave, presence)

This keeps dragging and editing responsive while still supporting real-time collaboration.
